title: HotFuzz: Discovering Algorithmic Denial-of-Service Vulnerabilities Through Guided Micro-Fuzzing
venue: Proceedings 2020 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record, 2020); arXiv API 2002.03416 (comment field: NDSS 2020, San Diego; DOI matches). Page numbers not in Crossref record (null).
solution: HotFuzz is a framework that finds algorithmic-complexity (AC) vulnerabilities in Java libraries by micro-fuzzing individual methods. A genetic algorithm evolves Java objects to trigger worst-case performance. Confirmed cases are replayed as standalone Java programs.
methodology: Abstract only. Micro-fuzzing with a genetic algorithm over Java objects; seed inputs derived by Small Recursive Instantiation (SRI); candidate witnesses are synthesized into Java programs and monitored for high CPU utilization. Evaluated on the JRE, the 100 most popular Maven libraries and DARPA STAC challenges, comparing SRI seeds against empty-value seeds.
results: Per abstract: verified known AC vulnerabilities, found previously unknown ones reported to vendors (confirmed by IBM and Oracle), and SRI seeds outperformed empty seeds. Abstract gives no counts.
gap: Our assessment: finds implementation-level worst-case inputs but gives no exact probability law; it does not treat keyed hashing, probe limits or stack-ordered deletion in a hash table.

title: Tuple Space Explosion: A Denial-of-Service Attack against a Software Packet Classifier
venue: Proceedings of the 15th International Conference on Emerging Networking Experiments and Technologies (CoNEXT '19)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.1145/3359989.3365431: title 'Tuple space explosion', subtitle 'a denial-of-service attack against a software packet classifier', pages 292-304, issued 2019-12-03); abstract text from Semantic Scholar record for the same DOI.
solution: Shows that the Tuple Space Search packet classifier used in Open vSwitch can be pushed into a denial of service by low-rate adversarial traffic (the Tuple Space Explosion attack). Proposes MFCGuard as a short-term countermeasure and suggests algorithms such as HaRP as a long-term fix.
methodology: Abstract only. Evaluates the TSS algorithm's space/time complexity under attacker-chosen headers; analyses cases with and without partial knowledge of the policy. Does not state the testbed in the abstract.
results: Per abstract: switch performance degraded to about 12% of capacity at 0.7 Mbps; with partial policy knowledge the target can be brought virtually down at the same rate; no complete mitigation known for TSS.
gap: Our assessment: a network-software complexity attack on a hash-based classifier, empirical in nature; it motivates adversarial thinking but offers no exact refusal-probability law, probe limit or key-lifetime rule.

title: Cryptanalysis of Reduced-Round SipHash
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.1093/comjnl/bxad026: vol 67, issue 3, pp. 875-883; online date 2023-03-21; Crossref issued date is 2023 (online)); abstract from Semantic Scholar record (also IACR ePrint 2019/865 per earlier search result).
solution: Truncated-differential cryptanalysis of reduced-round SipHash, the keyed short-input PRF used against hash flooding. Builds distinguishers for SipHash-2-1 and SipHash-2-2 and a key-recovery method for SipHash-2-1.
methodology: Abstract only. Exhaustive testing of all 1-bit input differences to find the largest output-bit biases after 3 or 4 SipRounds; links the bias to the difference after the first modular addition, which depends on key bits.
results: Per abstract: practical distinguishers at complexity 2^12 (SipHash-2-1) and 2^36 (SipHash-2-2, ignoring padding rules); about 97% of random keys recoverable for SipHash-2-1 at complexity 2^83. Reduced-round results only; full SipHash-2-4 is not attacked.
gap: Our assessment: supports the need to bound how long a key is used and how many outputs are exposed, but gives no hash-table-level guarantee; we should treat the PRF as an idealised assumption and cite this only as limits of that assumption.

title: Areion: Highly-Efficient Permutations and Its Applications to Hash Functions for Short Input
venue: IACR Transactions on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record: TCHES 2023, issue 2, pp. 115-154); abstract from Semantic Scholar record.
solution: Designs Areion, a family of wide-block permutations built on AES instructions, and derives hash functions for short inputs from them. Aimed at inputs up to about 2 KB, such as packets.
methodology: Abstract only. Permutation design leveraging AES instructions; benchmarked on Intel IceLake, Tiger Lake, Alder Lake and mobile platforms (Pixel 6, iPhone 13).
results: Per abstract: under 3 cycles per byte on the latest Intel for any message size, and about 10 times faster than state-of-the-art for messages up to about 100 bytes.
gap: Our assessment: shows fast short-input keyed/unkeyed hashing is practical, relevant to the cost side of a key-lifetime rule; it does not analyse hash tables or adversarial security of table behaviour. The abstract does not say whether the hashes are keyed.

title: Bloom Filters in Adversarial Environments
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.1145/3306193: TALG 15(3), pp. 1-30, issued 2019-06-07; Crossref lists the second author as 'Eylon, Yogev', a given/family swap, corrected here); arXiv API 1412.8356 (authors Moni Naor, Eylon Yogev). Conference version: CRYPTO 2015 (Crossref 10.1007/978-3-662-48000-7_28).
solution: Defines an adversarial model in which an adversary picks inputs and queries adaptively from earlier answers, and relates secure Bloom filters to cryptography. Gives a construction against query-bounded unbounded adversaries.
methodology: Abstract only. Cryptographic reductions and information-theoretic constructions for computationally bounded and query-bounded unbounded adversaries.
results: Per abstract: non-trivial Bloom filters against efficient adversaries exist iff one-way functions exist; against t queries a filter with O(n log(1/eps) + t) bits exists, versus n log(1/eps) for non-adaptive adversaries.
gap: Our assessment: sets the adaptive-adversary framework we can borrow, but treats approximate membership, not open-addressing tables; no exact finite-size refusal law and no deletion model.

title: Probabilistic Data Structures in Adversarial Environments
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '19)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record: pp. 1317-1334, issued 2019-11-06); abstract from Semantic Scholar record.
solution: Gives a provable-security treatment of probabilistic data structures when data and queries may depend on internal randomness. Shows that salts or secret keys yield provable security with little overhead.
methodology: Abstract only. A syntax covering many structures and security notions that support error bounds under powerful attacks; focuses on Bloom filters, also counting Bloom filters and count-min sketch.
results: Per abstract: findings for the traditional (unkeyed) structures are largely negative; simple keyed or salted variants give provable security at little overhead.
gap: Our assessment: close in spirit to our key-lifetime question, but for approximate-membership/sketch structures; does not give exact probe-limit refusal probabilities or handle stack-ordered undo.

title: Adversarial Correctness and Privacy for Probabilistic Data Structures
venue: Proceedings of the 2022 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '22)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record: pp. 1037-1050, issued 2022-11-07; first author spelled 'Filic' there, 'Filić' used here, with the diacritic seen in another Crossref record of the same author); arXiv id 2209.06955 from Semantic Scholar externalIds, abstract from Semantic Scholar (arXiv listing not fetched directly).
solution: Gives simulation-based definitions of correctness and privacy for approximate-membership structures, and proves Bloom and insertion-only Cuckoo filters can be protected by replacing or composing hashes with keyed PRFs.
methodology: Abstract only. Simulation-based security definitions applied to Bloom filters and insertion-only Cuckoo filters; practical storage and computation overhead of secure instances examined.
results: Per abstract: provable protection via keyed PRFs; overhead on storage and computation quantified (numbers not in the abstract).
gap: Our assessment: covers insertion-only Cuckoo filters, which are hash-table-like, but not deletions or exact finite-size refusal probabilities; supports using keyed PRFs as the model for our key-lifetime rules.

title: A Framework for Adversarially Robust Streaming Algorithms
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.1145/3498334: JACM 69(2), pp. 1-33, issued 2022-01-31; a SIGMOD Record version 10.1145/3471485.3471488 also exists); arXiv API 2003.14265 (abstract).
solution: Gives generic tools that turn non-robust randomized streaming algorithms into adversarially robust ones against adaptive adversaries who see outputs. Covers distinct elements, F_p estimation, heavy hitters and entropy.
methodology: Abstract only. Generic transformations for insertion-only streams, yielding robust (1+eps)-approximations.
results: Per abstract: space matches the best non-robust algorithms up to a poly(log n, 1/eps) factor, in some cases up to a constant.
gap: Our assessment: the adaptive-adversary model for sketches, not for dictionaries with deletions; offers no exact refusal probabilities for probe-limited tables.

title: Compact Frequency Estimators in Adversarial Environments
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '23)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record: pp. 3254-3268, issued 2023-11-15; author spelled 'Filic' there); abstract from Semantic Scholar record (abstract text truncated at 1800 characters in my fetch).
solution: Shows Count-Min Sketch and HeavyKeeper can be forced into large estimation errors by adaptive attacks, and proposes Count-Keeper, a composition of the two with suspicious-estimate flagging.
methodology: Abstract only. Attacks analysed analytically and experimentally, with tight agreement reported; Count-Keeper evaluated against honest and attacked streams.
results: Per abstract: significant errors forced on CMS and HK; Count-Keeper typically at least twice as accurate as CMS on honest streams and harder to attack.
gap: Our assessment: pairs exact analysis with experiments for an adaptive-attack setting, a model for our methodology; but concerns sketches, not probe-limited open addressing.

title: Linear Probing Revisited: Tombstones Mark the Demise of Primary Clustering
venue: 2021 IEEE 62nd Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.1109/focs52979.2021.00115: title with 'Demise', pp. 1171-1182; Crossref issued date 2022-02 is the proceedings publication date, conference was 2021); arXiv API 2107.01250 (v1 title says 'Death'; the final title uses 'Demise').
solution: Shows that tombstone deletions create an anti-clustering effect in linear probing, so amortized cost per operation stays about O~(x) at load 1-Theta(1/x). Introduces graveyard hashing, which removes primary clustering for any operation sequence.
methodology: Abstract only. Asymptotic analysis of linear probing under insertions and deletions; the abstract also states an external-memory block-transfer guarantee.
results: Per abstract: expected amortized cost O~(x) with tombstones; graveyard hashing gives expected cost O(x) at load 1-1/x; 1+o(1) block transfers when x = o(B).
gap: Our assessment: the closest prior work on linear probing with deletions, but asymptotic cost, not exact finite-size refusal probabilities under a probe limit, and no stack-ordered exact-undo discipline.

title: Parking Functions: From Combinatorics to Probability
venue: Methodology and Computing in Applied Probability
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record: vol 25, issue 1, article number 32, issued 2023-02-18); arXiv API 2103.17180 (abstract).
solution: Studies parking functions PF(m,n) with m cars and n spots: bijections to rooted spanning forests, an identity between the inversion and displacement enumerators, and the law of a single coordinate of a uniform parking function.
methodology: Abstract only. Bijective combinatorics, Tutte-polynomial correspondence, and adaptation of known random-linear-probe results to obtain covariances when m=n.
results: Per abstract: formula for the law of a single coordinate, a recurrence for the displacement enumerator, and the covariance of two coordinates when m=n.
gap: Our assessment: exact finite-size parking-function laws that underlie linear probing without a probe limit; no refusal after a probe limit, no deletions.

title: Parking Functions: Interdisciplinary Connections
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.1017/apr.2022.49: AAP 55(3), pp. 768-792, issued 2023-01-17); arXiv API 2107.01767 (abstract).
solution: Studies probabilistic properties of a uniform parking function, giving the joint law of multiple coordinates for m close to n (m below n asymptotically) and all covariances. Also studies interval parking functions.
methodology: Abstract only. Combinatorial construction called a parking function multi-shuffle; bijections between interval parking functions and edge-labeled spanning trees.
results: Per abstract: law of multiple coordinates and all covariances (two coordinates, a coordinate and an unattempted spot, two unattempted spots), contrasting the m close to n regime with m=n.
gap: Our assessment: exact and asymptotic laws for filled parking sequences, useful for the no-limit baseline; no probe limit, refusals or deletions.

title: Two-Way Linear Probing Revisited
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.3390/a16110500: Algorithms 16(11), article 500, issued 2023-10-28); arXiv API 2309.05308 (abstract).
solution: Introduces linear probing hash schemes using two probe sequences so that, at constant load factor, worst-case unsuccessful search time is O(log log n) almost surely. Gives matching lower bounds on maximum cluster size.
methodology: Abstract only. Probabilistic analysis of maximum cluster size for schemes with two linear probe sequences.
results: Per abstract: a.s. O(log log n) worst-case unsuccessful search at constant load; matching lower bounds on maximum cluster size for any algorithm using two linear probe sequences.
gap: Our assessment: bounds maximum cluster/probe length asymptotically but without exact finite-size laws, probe-limit refusals or deletions.

title: Quadratic Probing Revisited: Smoothed Analysis and the Fall of Robin Hood
verified_against: arXiv API only (id 2607.13247v1, published 2026-07-14). No Crossref record found; preprint, not peer reviewed as far as I could confirm. DOI null.
solution: Analyses a smoothed variant of quadratic probing under Robin Hood and anti-Robin Hood orderings, showing a separation in expected query time at load 1-eps. Extends to degree-d probing and fixed-offset sequences.
methodology: Abstract only. Smoothed analysis plus the probabilistic method for existence of good fixed-offset probe sequences.
results: Per abstract: anti-Robin Hood gives Theta(log 1/eps) while Robin Hood gives Theta(eps^(-1/2)); generalises to degree-d probing: O(max(log 1/eps, eps^(1-2/d))) for anti-Robin Hood and Theta(eps^(-1/d)) for Robin Hood.
gap: Our assessment: recent Robin Hood analysis for open addressing, concerning expected query time at high load; not linear probing refusals, deletions, or adversaries.
